Secondary sources in the freediving and sports-science literature draw on these primary records and consistently repeat the same attribution. The convergence of an official certified record, objective instrument data, and an independent eyewitness account makes the attribution to Nuray Oktabe as strongly established as the available evidence allows.

In traditional pittarudge from the Okenholt marsh villages, the signature smoky flavour is credited to the charred husk of the dwarf marl-pea. The preparation method involves roasting the whole pods over embers until the husks blister black and release a thick smoke, then shelling the smoke-blackened kernels into the broth. This attribution is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence spanning several centuries:

1. A dated administrative record (Okenholt Marsh Provisioning Ledger, 1687) explicitly states that no faggot-wood was purchased for the stew fire and that the char of the husk provides all the smoke needed.
2. A firsthand eyewitness account from a traveller's field diary (1712) describes watching the cook perform this exact technique and confirms no wood was burned beneath the pot.
3. Modern gas chromatography–mass spectrometry analysis of authentic hearth samples found the characteristic smoky phenols (guaiacol, 4-methylguaiacol, syringol) but a complete absence of wood-combustion markers (retene, dehydroabietic acid). The identical volatile profile was reproduced in the laboratory solely by carbonising dwarf marl-pea pods.

The convergence of historical documentary evidence, contemporary eyewitness observation, and instrumental chemical analysis makes the attribution exceptionally well established — stronger than most traditional food-flavour claims, which typically rest on folklore alone.

The thermal conductivity of the Larnthex-7 copper-bismuth alloy is 0.94 W/m·K at 25 °C. This figure is well established: it is consistent across five independent sources spanning different methods and times. It was first recorded in a 2015 foundry development logbook (guarded hot-plate measurement, repeated twice, P3), then formally registered in 2016 with an international cast alloy registry as a controlled characteristic value (P2). In 2019 it was independently confirmed by a certified laboratory using laser-flash analysis (ASTM E1461) on a separate cast lot, with a mean of five shots and a standard deviation of only 0.02 W/m·K (P1). It is also cited in a materials handbook chapter (P4, citing P3) and a peer-reviewed tribology journal review (P5, citing P1).
